grammar.title: Grammatica
grammar.rule: io porto → tu porti → Paolo porta; io ho → tu hai; io sono → tu sei.
grammar.note_en:
Io means “I”, and tu means “you” when addressing one familiar person. The ending of the verb also identifies that person. This chapter shows a common present-tense pattern: io porto (“I carry”), tu porti (“you carry”), Paolo porta (“Paolo carries”). The present describes an action now or a regular situation: io abito qui means “I live here”. These verbs belong to the group whose dictionary form ends in -are; this chapter teaches the actual singular endings -o, -i and -a, not every Italian verb pattern.

The reference rows read: porto/porti/porta (“I carry / you carry / carries”), cerco/cerchi/cerca (“I look for / you look for / looks for”), parlo/parli/parla (“I speak / you speak / speaks”), aspetto/aspetti/aspetta (“I wait / you wait / waits”). Cerchi has an h to preserve the hard c sound before i. These are statements and questions, not commands. Tu aspetti qui? asks “Are you waiting here?”; the same present form can make a request in context. Io cerco dentro la cucina means “I look inside the kitchen”; tu cerchi l’attrezzo means “you look for the tool”. The bedroom is camera here; stanza is the general word “room”.

Essere (“be”) and avere (“have”) do not use those regular endings: io sono (“I am”), tu sei (“you are”), Lei è (“you are”, formal); io ho (“I have”), tu hai (“you have”), Lei ha (“you have”, formal). Ho, hai and ha all have a silent h. Sono already meant “are” with plural subjects; with io it means “am”. Read the subject and situation together. Io sono Elena means “I am Elena”; tu sei Paolo means “you are Paolo”; io ho una casa piccola means “I have a small house”; tu hai una casa grande means “you have a large house”.

Elena uses Lei to address Paolo’s mother politely: Lei lavora qui? means “Do you work here?” The verb has the same form as with one named person. This use of Lei means “you”, not “she”; capitalization helps signal the courteous address. Paolo uses tu with his mother and with Elena. The mother uses tu with her son and Lei with Elena. The story does not yet require you to produce plural verb persons.

The possessive still agrees with its noun: il suo attrezzo means “his tool” in the narration about Paolo. The named addressee and story context identify the relationship. Singular padre normally omits the article with an unmodified possessive: mio padre, “my father”. Mamma allows variation; this story uses mia mamma, “my mum”. The definite descriptions la mamma di Paolo and il padre di Paolo mean “Paolo’s mother” and “Paolo’s father”. Leaving their boxes in place makes respect for ownership part of the action, rather than another form recital.
